title: Ἀλώπηξ καὶ πίθηκος ⟨περὶ εὐγενείας ἐρίζοντες⟩
titleEn: The Fox and the Monkey Quarrelling over Ancestry
part: The Fox and the Monkey Quarrelling over Ancestry (Chambry 39)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 39. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« », ⟨ ⟩ for editorial supplements). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλώπηξ καὶ πίθηκος ἐν ταὐτῷ ὁδοιποροῦντες περὶ εὐγενείας ἤριζον.
sentences.tr: Alōpēx kai pithēkos en tautōi hodoiporountes peri eugeneias ērizon.
sentences.l: A fox and a monkey, travelling in the same place, were quarrelling about good birth.
sentences.i: A fox and a monkey were journeying together and quarrelling about good birth.
sentences.n: ἐν ταὐτῷ is a crasis of ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ, “in the same place” — hence together. The participle ὁδοιποροῦντες is masculine plural although one of the pair is grammatically feminine: a mixed pair takes the masculine. The opening line repeats fable 35 almost word for word.

sentences.t: Πολλὰ δὲ ἑκατέρου διεξιόντος, ἐπειδὴ ἐγένοντο κατά τινα τόπον, ἐνταῦθα ἀποβλέψας ἀνεστέναξεν ὁ πίθηκος.
sentences.tr: Polla de hekaterou diexiontos, epeidē egenonto kata tina topon, entautha apoblepsas anestenaxen ho pithēkos.
sentences.l: And each of the two going through many things, when they came to a certain place, the monkey, looking over there, groaned aloud.
sentences.i: Each had a great deal to say; and when they came to a certain spot, the monkey looked across at it and let out a groan.
sentences.n: Another genitive absolute, ἑκατέρου διεξιόντος, with the same verb διεξιέναι, “to go through an account at length,” that the crocodile used in fable 35. The aorist ἀνεστέναξεν is one groan, not a habit of groaning.

sentences.t: Τῆς δὲ ἀλώπεκος ἐρομένης τὴν αἰτίαν, ὁ πίθηκος ἐπιδείξας αὐτῇ τὰ μνήματα, εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ οὐ μέλλω κλάειν, ὁρῶν τὰς στήλας τῶν πατρικῶν μου ἀπελευθέρων καὶ δούλων ; »
sentences.tr: Tēs de alōpekos eromenēs tēn aitian, ho pithēkos epideixas autēi ta mnēmata, eipen· « All’ ou mellō klaein, horōn tas stēlas tōn patrikōn mou apeleutherōn kai doulōn ; »
sentences.l: And the fox asking the reason, the monkey, having pointed out to her the tombs, said: « But am I not bound to weep, seeing the gravestones of my father's freedmen and slaves? »
sentences.i: When the fox asked why, the monkey pointed out the tombs to her and said, “How should I not weep, seeing the gravestones of my father's freedmen and slaves?”
sentences.n: The boast is one of property. ἀπελεύθεροι are slaves formally set free; a graveyard full of a household's freedmen and slaves advertises a large and long-established house. στῆλαι are the upright inscribed slabs set over Greek graves. μέλλω with the infinitive here carries the sense “am I not to…?” — the indignant rhetorical question.

sentences.t: Κἀκείνη πρὸς αὐτὸν ἔφη· « Ἀλλὰ ψεύδου ὅσα βούλει· οὐδεὶς γὰρ τούτων ἀναστὰς ἐλέγξει σε. »
sentences.tr: Kakeinē pros auton ephē· « Alla pseudou hosa boulei· oudeis gar toutōn anastas elenxei se. »
sentences.l: And she said to him: « Well, lie as much as you wish; for none of these will stand up and refute you. »
sentences.n: Κἀκείνη is a crasis of καὶ ἐκείνη. ψεύδου is a present middle imperative — “go on lying.” The aorist participle ἀναστάς does the work of a whole clause: none of them will get up to contradict him. ἐλέγξει is the same root as the ἔλεγχος of fable 35 — the refutation that facts, or witnesses, supply.

sentences.t: Οὕτω καὶ τῶν ἀνθρώπων οἱ ψευδολόγοι τότε μάλιστα καταλαζονεύονται, ὅταν τοὺς ἐλέγχοντας μὴ ἔχωσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtō kai tōn anthrōpōn hoi pseudologoi tote malista katalazoneuontai, hotan tous elenchontas mē echōsin.
sentences.l: So too the liars among men then most of all play the braggart, whenever they do not have those who would refute them.
sentences.i: So too the liars among men brag most freely just when there is nobody by to contradict them.
sentences.n: ὅταν with the subjunctive (ἔχωσιν) states a general rule rather than one occasion — “whenever.” καταλαζονεύεσθαι is built on ἀλαζών, the boastful impostor of Greek comedy. The frame τότε μάλιστα … ὅταν, “then most of all … whenever,” is a favourite shape in these morals.
